title: Respiratory Infection in the Immunocompromised Host: Broaden the Differential, Escalate Earlier
bottomLine: Immunocompromised patients can deteriorate with muted fever, leukocytosis or radiographic findings. Define the immune defect and tempo, assess oxygenation and organ dysfunction early, obtain source-directed microbiology/imaging promptly, and involve acute-care/infectious-disease/respirology pathways sooner than in an uncomplicated community respiratory infection.
recognize: Risk depends on the type and depth of immune suppression: neutropenia, transplant, corticosteroids, biologics, hematologic malignancy, HIV and other immune defects create different pathogen profiles.
Hypoxemia, tachypnea, new infiltrates, cough, dyspnea or subtle functional decline may be the first clues even when fever is absent.
differentiate: Bacterial pneumonia, viral disease, Pneumocystis, fungal infection, tuberculosis/NTM, drug pneumonitis, pulmonary edema, hemorrhage and malignancy can overlap.
A normal or nonspecific early chest x-ray does not safely exclude serious lower-respiratory disease in a high-risk host.
assessment: Identify the exact immunosuppressive condition/drugs, neutrophil status, transplant timing, prophylaxis, prior organisms, travel/exposures and recent antimicrobials.
Assess oxygen saturation, respiratory effort, hemodynamics and mental status before focusing on pathogen identification.
workup: Use CBC/differential, renal/hepatic function, blood/respiratory cultures or molecular testing and chest imaging according to severity and immune defect.
CT, bronchoscopy or specialized fungal/Pneumocystis testing may be required when routine testing is nondiagnostic; specialist guidance should shape invasive sampling.
management: Hospitalize/escalate patients with hypoxemia, instability, neutropenia with significant respiratory illness, rapidly progressive imaging or inability to maintain oral therapy.
Select empiric therapy from immune defect, severity, prior microbiology, prophylaxis and local resistance rather than routine CAP therapy alone.
De-escalate or redirect treatment once microbiology and clinical response clarify the cause.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic dysfunction and interactions with transplant, oncology or antiretroviral therapy can materially change antimicrobial selection/dose.
Do not start corticosteroids for presumed inflammatory pneumonitis until serious infection has been considered and the indication is clinically supported.
counselling: Teach high-risk patients to seek care early for new dyspnea, persistent fever, oxygen change or significant cough rather than waiting for classic pneumonia symptoms.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures, molecular tests and imaging; review prophylaxis/vaccination and immunosuppression changes with the specialty team after recovery.
examTrap: Sending an immunocompromised patient home because the temperature and WBC are normal despite new hypoxemia and dyspnea.
oneLinePearl: In immune suppression, absence of fever is not absence of danger.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2026 infection-screening before ILD immunosuppression statement
Canadian infectious-disease and transplant/oncology respiratory practice

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Screen High-Risk Asymptomatic Patients, Diagnose Symptoms
bottomLine: Lung-cancer screening is for asymptomatic people at sufficiently high smoking-related risk and uses low-dose CT through an evidence-based program/pathway. Hemoptysis, persistent unexplained cough, weight loss or another cancer symptom requires diagnostic evaluation instead of being routed through a screening algorithm.
recognize: Current Canadian screening access and risk thresholds vary by national recommendation and provincial program; smoking history remains the major eligibility driver.
Low-dose CT is the screening modality; chest x-ray and sputum cytology are not effective lung-cancer screening tests.
differentiate: Screening applies before symptoms; a symptomatic patient has a diagnostic problem even if they also meet screening eligibility.
An incidental nodule discovered outside screening follows an incidental-nodule pathway rather than automatically the organized screening schedule.
assessment: Document age, current/former smoking exposure accurately, years smoked/quit timing, prior lung cancer, comorbidity/frailty and whether the patient could undergo meaningful diagnostic treatment if cancer were found.
Ask explicitly about hemoptysis, persistent/progressive cough, unexplained weight loss, chest pain and other alarm symptoms before calling the encounter screening.
workup: Refer eligible asymptomatic patients to the current provincial/territorial organized screening or validated LDCT pathway.
For symptoms, order diagnostic imaging/workup based on the presentation rather than a screening LDCT order.
management: Use shared decision-making about screening benefit, false positives, incidental findings, overdiagnosis and cumulative radiation.
Provide smoking-cessation support regardless of whether the patient accepts or qualifies for screening.
Ensure abnormal screening findings are tracked through the program/nodule diagnostic pathway until resolved.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary invasive procedures or contrast studies before the screening/nodule risk pathway warrants them; consider renal, allergy and bleeding risk for downstream diagnostics.
counselling: Explain that screening is not a guarantee and is not the same as evaluating symptoms.
Use non-stigmatizing smoking-history language and offer cessation treatment without making screening contingent on quitting.
followUp: Confirm enrolment/completion and ownership of abnormal results; do not assume the screening program automatically closes every incidental finding.
examTrap: Ordering a 'screening' LDCT for a patient with hemoptysis instead of starting a diagnostic lung-cancer workup.
oneLinePearl: No symptoms = screening pathway; symptoms = diagnostic pathway.
sourceBasis: Canadian Cancer Society lung-cancer screening resources

title: Chronic Cough: Start With Red Flags, Exposures, Medication, and Common Causes
bottomLine: Chronic cough is a symptom with a structured differential, not a diagnosis. First exclude alarm features and review smoking/vaping, occupational exposure, ACE-inhibitor use and chest imaging/clinical context; then evaluate common upper-airway, asthma/eosinophilic and reflux-related causes without stacking multiple empiric therapies indefinitely.
recognize: Upper-airway symptoms, variable wheeze/airflow, reflux features, medication exposure and smoking history are common diagnostic clues.
Multiple causes can coexist, so partial response does not always prove one diagnosis.
differentiate: Hemoptysis, weight loss, persistent fever, focal chest findings, hypoxemia or a high-risk smoking history require malignancy/infection/structural evaluation rather than routine empiric treatment.
ACE-inhibitor cough can occur without wheeze and may persist for a period after discontinuation.
assessment: Document duration, dry/productive pattern, triggers, nocturnal/exertional features, rhinitis/sinus symptoms, reflux, dysphagia/aspiration, medications, tobacco/vaping/cannabis and occupational/home exposures.
Examine upper airway, chest and cardiopulmonary status; assess red flags before calling the cough uncomplicated.
workup: Use chest radiography and spirometry when indicated by the chronic-cough pathway and risk profile.
Escalate to CT, methacholine/eosinophilic testing, ENT/GI evaluation or specialty referral when the common-cause pathway fails or red flags are present.
management: Treat the supported cause with a defined therapeutic trial and endpoint rather than adding several empiric medications simultaneously.
Remove cough-provoking exposure/ACE inhibitor when clinically appropriate and reassess.
Refer unexplained refractory cough, abnormal imaging, significant hemoptysis or physiologic impairment.
medicationSafety: Avoid repeated antibiotics for chronic cough without a bacterial syndrome.
Avoid routine opioid antitussive use, especially in older adults or with other sedatives, because benefit is limited and harm can be substantial.
counselling: Explain that cough treatment is often sequential because several common causes can mimic each other; set a specific reassessment date for each trial.
followUp: Document response to each targeted intervention and reopen the differential if the expected response does not occur.
examTrap: Treating chronic cough with repeated antibiotics or PPIs forever without checking ACE-inhibitor use, smoking/exposures, spirometry and chest imaging/red flags.
oneLinePearl: Chronic cough needs a sequence: red flags, exposure/medication review, common causes, then targeted escalation.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society cough toolkit/current respiratory practice

title: Allergic Rhinitis and Rhinosinusitis: Separate Inflammation From Bacterial Infection
bottomLine: Most nasal/sinus symptoms are allergic or viral/inflammatory rather than bacterial. Diagnose by symptom pattern and duration, use intranasal anti-inflammatory therapy and allergen strategies appropriately, and reserve antibiotics for a compatible acute bacterial rhinosinusitis pattern rather than coloured discharge alone.
recognize: Allergic rhinitis commonly causes sneezing, itching, clear rhinorrhea and congestion with seasonal/perennial triggers.

Acute viral rhinosinusitis commonly improves without antibiotics; bacterial disease is suggested by a compatible severe, persistent or worsening-after-initial-improvement course rather than one symptom alone.
differentiate: Facial pressure and coloured mucus can occur in viral disease and are not stand-alone proof of bacterial sinusitis.
Unilateral obstruction/bleeding, orbital symptoms or recurrent atypical disease requires a structural/ENT differential.
assessment: Assess duration/trajectory, allergy triggers, asthma, medication use, fever/severity, dental symptoms, unilateral findings and prior recurrent episodes.
Review pregnancy, glaucoma/BPH concerns and other factors that affect decongestant/antihistamine choice.
workup: Routine sinus imaging is not needed for uncomplicated acute rhinosinusitis.
Allergy testing, CT or ENT evaluation is reserved for selected persistent/recurrent, surgical, immune-deficient or atypical cases.
management: Use intranasal corticosteroid, saline and appropriate antihistamine/allergen management for allergic rhinitis.
Provide symptomatic care for viral rhinosinusitis and prescribe antibiotics only when the clinical bacterial pattern and patient factors justify them.
Address asthma control because upper- and lower-airway disease commonly interact.
medicationSafety: Topical decongestant overuse can cause rebound congestion; systemic decongestants can worsen hypertension, palpitations or urinary symptoms.
Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum antibiotics and prolonged courses without reassessment.
counselling: Teach intranasal spray technique and explain why coloured mucus does not automatically mean antibiotics are needed.
followUp: Reassess persistent/recurrent disease and refer if complications, structural disease or refractory symptoms are suspected.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics solely because sinus drainage is green without considering duration and illness trajectory.
oneLinePearl: Rhinosinusitis becomes bacterial by its clinical course, not by mucus colour.

title: Acute Bronchitis vs Pneumonia: Use Vitals and Lung Findings Before Antibiotics
bottomLine: Acute bronchitis is usually viral and does not benefit from routine antibiotics. Pneumonia becomes more likely with abnormal vital signs, focal lung findings, hypoxemia, systemic illness or high-risk host features; order chest imaging when the probability is meaningful rather than because the cough is severe or sputum is coloured.
recognize: Bronchitis commonly causes acute cough after a viral syndrome, sometimes with wheeze or sputum colour change.
Pneumonia is more concerning with fever, tachypnea, hypoxemia, focal crackles/bronchial breath sounds, pleuritic pain or significant systemic illness.
differentiate: Sputum colour does not reliably distinguish viral bronchitis from bacterial pneumonia.
Older/frail or immunocompromised patients can have pneumonia without high fever and need a lower threshold for imaging/escalation.
assessment: Check temperature, respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate, BP, work of breathing and focal chest findings.
Assess age/frailty, immune status, aspiration risk, comorbidity, recent healthcare exposure and duration/trajectory.
workup: Avoid chest x-ray in a low-risk patient with normal vital signs and normal lung exam when pneumonia probability is very low.
Use chest imaging and cause-directed testing when vitals/exam, host risk or clinical course makes pneumonia plausible.
management: Treat uncomplicated acute bronchitis supportively and set expectations that cough can persist beyond the first several days.
Treat confirmed/likely pneumonia according to current Canadian/local guidance, severity and comorbidity, with appropriate follow-up.
Escalate hypoxemia, instability, sepsis or inability to maintain hydration/oral therapy.
medicationSafety: Routine antibiotics for bronchitis cause adverse effects and resistance without meaningful benefit.
Avoid codeine/other sedative cough suppressants in high-risk patients when respiratory depression, delirium or falls are concerns.
counselling: Explain why a severe cough or green sputum does not automatically require antibiotics, and give return precautions for dyspnea, persistent fever, confusion or worsening course.
followUp: Reassess if symptoms worsen after initial improvement, persist unexpectedly, or new pneumonia red flags develop.
examTrap: Prescribing antibiotics for acute bronchitis because sputum is green while ignoring normal vitals and lung examination.
oneLinePearl: Bronchitis vs pneumonia is a physiology/exam decision, not a sputum-colour decision.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada Cold Standard/respiratory stewardship

title: Obstructive Sleep Apnea: Diagnose Objectively, Then Make PAP Usable
bottomLine: Obstructive sleep apnea is suspected clinically but diagnosed with appropriate sleep testing. Severity, symptoms, cardiovascular risk, occupation/driving risk and patient preference guide treatment; PAP works only if interface, pressure, humidification and adherence barriers are actively managed rather than simply issuing a machine.
recognize: Loud snoring, witnessed apneas/gasping, nonrestorative sleep, morning headache and excessive daytime sleepiness are common clues.
OSA can present with resistant hypertension, atrial fibrillation, nocturia, mood/cognitive symptoms or safety-critical sleepiness rather than a classic complaint.
differentiate: Insomnia, insufficient sleep, circadian disorder, depression, sedatives/alcohol, restless legs and central sleep apnea can mimic or coexist with OSA.
A screening questionnaire estimates risk but does not diagnose OSA.
assessment: Assess sleep schedule, snoring/apneas, daytime sleepiness, BMI/neck/airway features, cardiovascular disease, sedatives/alcohol, occupation and driving risk.
Ask about COPD, neuromuscular disease, heart failure or opioid use that may change the appropriate testing modality.
workup: Use home sleep apnea testing or attended polysomnography according to pretest probability, comorbidity and local sleep-medicine criteria.
Do not use overnight oximetry alone as a universal diagnostic substitute for OSA.
management: Offer PAP when indicated and troubleshoot mask leak, nasal symptoms, pressure intolerance, humidification and sleep behaviour early.
Weight-management support, positional therapy, oral appliance or selected surgical approaches may be appropriate depending on phenotype and preference.
Address dangerous sleepiness and occupational/driving safety immediately rather than waiting for long-term PAP response.
medicationSafety: Alcohol, opioids and other sedatives can worsen sleep-disordered breathing and daytime impairment; review their necessity and timing.
Do not prescribe sedative-hypnotics for 'poor sleep' before assessing untreated OSA when symptoms suggest it.
counselling: Explain that PAP benefit depends on regular use and that discomfort should trigger troubleshooting, not abandonment.
Discuss driving/work safety explicitly when daytime sleepiness is significant.
followUp: Review objective PAP usage, residual events/leak, symptoms and blood pressure/cardiovascular context; refer persistent intolerance or complex sleep-disordered breathing to sleep medicine.
examTrap: Diagnosing OSA from STOP-BANG alone—or issuing CPAP and never checking mask leak, residual events or persistent sleepiness.
oneLinePearl: Screening finds OSA risk; sleep testing diagnoses it; follow-up makes PAP effective.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society sleep-disordered breathing resources
